div.head: Shiji I: Basic Annals
div.p: Basic Annals of Qin: In the first year of King Xiaowen, he pardoned offenders, honoured the meritorious servants of the former kings, bestowed generous favour on his kinsmen, and opened the parks and preserves. When King Xiaowen had put off mourning, he came to the throne in October, on the day Jihai; on the third day, Xinchou, he died, and his son King Zhuangxiang was set up.

div.head: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses
div.p: Hereditary House of Zhao: In the sixteenth year, Lian Po besieged Yan. Yue Cheng was made Lord Wuxiang.

div.head: Shiji IV: Biographies
div.p: Biography of Lian Po and Lin Xiangru: Five years after the siege of Handan was raised, Yan adopted Li Fu's plan — "those of Zhao in their prime were all used up at Changping, and their orphans are not yet grown" — and raised troops to strike at Zhao. Zhao sent Lian Po in command; he struck and heavily defeated the Yan army at Hao, killed Li Fu, and went on to besiege Yan. Yan ceded five Fortresses and sued for peace, and this was granted. Zhao enfeoffed Lian Po with Weiwen as Lord Xinping and made him Acting Chancellor of State.

When Lian Po had been dismissed at Changping and returned home, in the time when he had lost his position, his old retainers all left. When he was again employed as general, the retainers came back again. Lian Po said: "Retainers, withdraw!" A retainer said: "Ah! How late you are in seeing it, my lord! All under Heaven make their friendships as in the market: when you have position I follow you, and when you have none I leave. That is the plain principle of it; what is there to resent?" After six years, Zhao sent Lian Po to attack Wei's Fanyang, and he took it.

div.head: Shiji V: Biographies
div.p: Biography of Lü Buwei: The King of Qin had been on the throne one year when he died; his posthumous title was Xiaowen. The Heir Apparent, Zichu, succeeded him; this was King Zhuangxiang. The one King Zhuangxiang had as his mother, Queen Huayang, became Queen Dowager Huayang, and his real mother, Lady Xia, was honoured as Queen Dowager Xia.

div.head: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I
div.p: The Zhao general Li Mu heavily defeated more than a hundred thousand Xiongnu horsemen, destroyed the Danlan, broke the Donghu, brought the Linhu to submission, and the Chanyu fled.
Analysis: Shiji, Biography of Lian Po and Lin Xiangru:

Li Mu was a fine general of Zhao's northern frontier. He was regularly stationed at Yanmen in Dai, on guard against the Xiongnu. He appointed officers at his own discretion, and the market taxes were all paid into his headquarters for the soldiers' expenses. Every day he slaughtered several oxen to feast his men; he drilled them in archery and riding, kept careful watch on the beacon fires, used many spies, and treated the fighting men generously. He laid down a rule: "When the Xiongnu come in to raid, withdraw at once into the strongholds; anyone who dares to take captives will be beheaded." Whenever the Xiongnu came in, the beacons gave careful warning and the men withdrew at once into the strongholds and did not dare to fight. So it went for several years, and nothing was lost either. But the Xiongnu took Li Mu for a coward, and even the Zhao frontier troops thought their general a coward. The King of Zhao reproved Li Mu, but Li Mu went on as before. The King of Zhao was angry, recalled him, and had another man take over the command.

After a year or more, whenever the Xiongnu came, the army went out to fight. Going out to fight, it was repeatedly worsted, the losses were many, and on the frontier there was no farming or herding. The king again asked for Li Mu. Mu shut his gate and would not come out, insisting that he was ill. The King of Zhao then pressed him again to rise and sent him to command the troops. Mu said: "If Your Majesty must employ your servant, your servant will dare to accept the command only if he may do as before." The king consented.

Li Mu arrived and kept to the old rule. For several years the Xiongnu got nothing, and to the end they took him for a coward. The frontier soldiers received rewards every day and were never used, and all of them wished for a single battle. Thereupon he fitted out picked chariots, and got thirteen hundred; picked horsemen, and got thirteen thousand; soldiers of the hundred jin of gold, fifty thousand; and bowmen, a hundred thousand; and he drilled them all for battle. He let the herds out to graze far and wide, and the people filled the open country. The Xiongnu came in with a small force; he feigned defeat and abandoned several thousand men to them. When the Chanyu heard of it, he came in at the head of a great host. Li Mu set many unexpected formations, spread out his left and right wings and struck, and heavily defeated and killed more than a hundred thousand Xiongnu horsemen. He destroyed the Danlan, broke the Donghu, brought the Linhu to submission, and the Chanyu fled. For more than ten years after that the Xiongnu did not dare to come near the frontier Fortresses of Zhao.

The Shiji, Hereditary House of Zhao, records Li Mu as general in the second year of King Daoxiang of Zhao (243 BC); the date of Li Mu's war with the Xiongnu is not known. Further, the Shiji, Account of the Xiongnu: "Later, in the time of the Zhao general Li Mu, the Xiongnu did not dare to enter the Zhao frontier."

Li Mu's war with the Xiongnu was perhaps after the second year of King Daoxiang of Zhao (243 BC). "For more than ten years after that" perhaps means the ten-odd years from King Daoxiang to Qin's destruction of Zhao.
